report.tagline: Amazon's live streaming site where gamers and other creators broadcast live and fans chat, subscribe and tip in real time.
report.simpleSummary: Twitch is a website and app where people stream live, mostly playing video games, but also chatting, cooking or making music. Viewers watch for free and talk with the streamer and each other in a live chat. Fans can pay a monthly subscription to a streamer or send 'Bits', which are small tips. Twitch and the streamer share that money, and Twitch also shows ads.

overview.whatItDoes: Twitch hosts live broadcasts from millions of creators and lets fans watch, chat and pay creators. It makes money from subscriptions, Bits and ads, and shares that money with streamers. It is owned by Amazon and linked to Prime Gaming, which gives one free subscription a month.
howItWorks: Anyone can stream with software like OBS or the Twitch app.
Viewers watch free and chat live; streamers react to chat in real time.
Fans subscribe monthly at three tiers, or gift subs to others.
Bits are bought by viewers and cheered in chat; streamers earn about 1 cent per Bit.
Ads run before and during streams; streamers can choose how many to run.
Prime Gaming members get one free sub a month to give to a streamer.
overview.valueProposition: For viewers: live, interactive entertainment and a sense of community with favourite streamers. For streamers: tools and an audience to earn a living from live content.

businessModel.summary: Twitch makes money from fan subscriptions, Bits and ads. It keeps a share of each sub and Bit, usually about half of subs, and pays the rest to streamers. Amazon owns Twitch and does not report its profit, but serving live video is expensive.

revenueStreams.detail: Tier 1, 2 and 3 subs, gifted subs and Prime Gaming subs. Twitch keeps about 30% to 50%.
Viewers buy Bits; Twitch keeps the margin above the 1 cent per Bit paid to streamers.
Pre-roll and mid-roll ads; streamers get a share.

businessModel.pricing: Free to watch. Subscriptions are $5.99, $9.99 and $24.99 a month in the US, with lower regional prices in India and other countries. Bits cost about $1.40 for 100.
businessModel.unitEconomics: On a $5.99 US sub with a 50/50 split, the streamer gets about $3. Twitch keeps about $3, minus payment or app store fees. Live video costs more to serve than recorded video because it must be sent instantly. A viewer who never pays earns Twitch only a little from ads. So Twitch depends on a small share of paying fans, which is why the split fight with streamers matters.

howTheyGetUsers: Clips shared on TikTok, X and YouTube
growth.moat: Twitch has the biggest live chat culture, with emotes, raids and community habits built over a decade. Fans follow streamers, and many streamers have stayed for the community. But big streamers can leave for better deals, and fans often follow them.

competitors.name: YouTube Live
competitors.positioning: Live streaming inside YouTube, now about half of all live hours watched.
competitors.howThisProductDiffers: Twitch has a stronger live chat culture; YouTube has better discovery and VODs.

competitors.name: Kick
competitors.positioning: Streaming site with a 95/5 sub split and big creator deals.
competitors.howThisProductDiffers: Twitch has a safer brand and more viewers; Kick pays streamers more.

competitors.name: TikTok LIVE
competitors.positioning: Live streaming in TikTok, strong on mobile and gifts.
competitors.howThisProductDiffers: Twitch is better for long gaming streams.

pmLessons: Creators are the supply. If top streamers leave for Kick or YouTube, their fans often follow.
The revenue split is a product decision. Paying creators more can cost margin today but protect the platform tomorrow.
Discovery decides whether new creators stay. A platform that only helps big streamers will slowly run out of new ones.
Owning a link to a big company helps. Prime Gaming free subs give Twitch money and users rivals cannot copy easily.

interviewQuestions.question: Kick offers streamers a 95/5 split. How should Twitch respond?
interviewQuestions.hint: Start with who is leaving and why: money, reach or rules. Model what a better split costs Twitch against the subs lost when a big streamer leaves. Suggest targeted offers, like better splits for growing streamers, plus non-cash value such as discovery and safety.

interviewQuestions.question: How would you improve discovery for small streamers?
interviewQuestions.hint: Define the problem with data: share of streams with zero viewers. List options like a clips feed, category spotlights and raids. Pick one, and measure new streamer retention and viewer satisfaction.

interviewQuestions.question: Twitch hours watched were flat while YouTube grew 15%. Diagnose it.
interviewQuestions.hint: Split hours into viewers times hours per viewer, then by category: gaming, Just Chatting, sports, esports. Check where YouTube grew (World Cup, sports) and whether Twitch lacks those rights or streamers.

interviewQuestions.question: Design a feature for big esports events on Twitch.
interviewQuestions.hint: Pick the user: casual fan or hardcore fan. Think about co-streams, multi-view, predictions and clips. Measure peak viewers, chat activity and new follows after the event.

interviewQuestions.question: How would you grow Twitch in India?
interviewQuestions.hint: Focus on mobile games like BGMI and Free Fire, Hindi and regional streamers, low regional sub prices and UPI payments. Compare with YouTube Live, which leads in India, and pick a niche to win.
